source_terms: benefit maximizers

money for value
value for money
item.claim: Bijapurkar proposes a segmentation whose axis is not spending power but VALUE ORIENTATION — how a buyer thinks about benefit against cost. Her five: the rich as benefit maximizers, oriented to "money for value", willing to pay more for more, described as "anywhere in the world consumers who just happen to be in India"; the consuming class as cost-benefit optimizers, oriented to "value for money", balancing the two continuously, "very hard to seduce with imagery-oriented brand benefits"; the climbers as cash-constrained benefit maximizers with a fixed price point who shop for the maximum available within it; the aspirants, new and therefore occasional consumers; and the destitute. She claims the model is generic — "this value orientation-based consumer class model is a generic Indian model that works for all businesses" — and demonstrates it across office automation, hospital services, cellphones, education, chemicals and farm equipment.

mechanism.text: Two buyers with the same budget can want opposite things from it: one to spend it all on the most benefit obtainable, another to spend as little of it as will do. Since the offer that wins differs between them while the affordability data does not distinguish them, a segmentation on spending power will place them together and mis-specify the offer for at least one.

scope.conditions: Presented as a generic Indian model applicable across consumer and industrial categories, on NCAER's consumer-classes framework as the underlying population data.

caveats.text: the claim that the model 'works for all businesses' is a strong universal, supported by a series of illustrative applications the author asserts rather than by any validation. No case is given where it failed, and no test is offered

the class labels (rich / consuming class / climbers / aspirants / destitute) come from NCAER; the VALUE-ORIENTATION overlay is the author's. The record keeps the two apart because the first is survey-derived and the second is not

the Nirma case that anchors the climbers segment is a well-known 1980s story told without figures beyond 'outselling it ten to one in tonnage terms', and the harshness of the product ('65 per cent soda ash') is reported as consumer-accepted on the basis of a single quoted rationalisation
population sizes attached to the segments are 2005-06 vintage and predate the period this project operates in

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: The population data is named and sourced; the value-orientation overlay is the author's and is unvalidated.

source_stated_remedies: segment on how the buyer trades benefit against cost, and design a portfolio spanning the resulting orientations

source_terms: The Law of the Generic
One of the fastest routes to failure is giving a brand a generic name.
The mind doesn't deal in letters or words. It deals in sounds.
item.claim: Law 12. A generic name cannot separate a brand from its competitors, and the authors ground this in a claim about processing. Most brand communication happens verbally rather than visually — they say the average person spends nine times as long listening to radio and television as reading print — and even the printed word is processed through the sound it generates, so a reader cannot hear the difference between "general" and "General". Capitalising a generic word does not make it a name. They use this to explain why line extensions fare poorly: an extension typically pairs a brand name with a generic descriptor, and the descriptor cannot create the separate identity the branding process needs.

mechanism.text: Sound is the channel. Because the mind processes the printed word through its sound, the orthographic marking that distinguishes a proper noun from a common one is lost, and the generic word is heard as generic however it is set. The naming process, the authors say, goes wrong because it is conducted visually — logotypes mounted on foamcore and passed round a boardroom — rather than by ear.

scope.conditions: the authors allow that some generic-named companies succeeded, and explain those separately

caveats.text: the nine-times listening-to-reading ratio is cited without source and is a claim about media time, not about how names are processed

the historical objection is handled by an alternative explanation the authors assert rather than test: National Biscuit, General Electric and International Harvester succeeded because they were first, 'in spite of their names'. Since success is credited to priority and failure to the name, the law cannot be disconfirmed by either outcome
the Vaseline Intensive Care case is conceded as a generic descriptor that became a brand, and explained as luck — customers happening to treat the descriptor as a name

source_stated_problems: the biggest mistake made when picking brand names. The process proceeds visually rather than verbally.
generic names disappear into the ether
source_stated_remedies: take a regular word and use it out of context to connote the primary attribute of your brand

positive.description: words used out of context — Blockbuster for video rental, Budget for car rental, Staples for office supplies, and Intel as a generic phrase cut in half

counter.description: the shelf of near-identical Nature's-something supplement brands, offered as names that cannot enter a mind

intra_source_relations.note: says which names can carry the Law of the Name's burden
supplies a naming reason line extensions fail
the same primacy of word over visual runs through the Law of Shape

item.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
item.source_locator: printed p. 24 (Ch. 5, 'you can't become generic by overtaking the leader')
item.question: A challenger brand outsells the category leader and its marketing director expects the brand name to become the generic term for the category. What boundary condition do the authors state, and what test do they give for whether a brand has actually got there?
item.answer: The boundary is absolute in their statement of it: you cannot become generic by overtaking the leader. A brand can own the category word only by having been the first brand and having established the category, and they say Pepsi would not become generic for cola even if it outsold Coke — noting that it once did outsell it in the supermarket distribution channel. Their test for whether a brand has the generic position is ordinary speech: people asking for a Xerox copy, a Q-Tip, Reynolds Wrap, Scotch tape, or asking someone to hand them a Kleenex while looking at a box of Scott tissue. The remedy they offer a brand that was not first is not to push harder on volume but to create a new category by narrowing the focus, and own the word there instead.
item.support: Printed p. 24 for the boundary and the speech test, pp. 24-25 for the narrowing remedy and the Federal Express illustration. No mechanism is given for why priority rather than usage fixes the generic term; the rule is stated and illustrated.
confounders: the trademark-law worry about genericide, which is a different concern — the authors treat generic status as an asset, not a risk
assuming heavy advertising can buy the position; the chapter's whole point is that it cannot be bought after the fact
confusing owning the category word with owning an attribute word — the authors treat Kleenex (category) and Prego's 'thick' (attribute) as two different routes

item.description: The four reasons the author himself gives, in one passage, for the saturation of Indian advertising with film and cricket stars: celebrity cost is small relative to media weight; celebrity credibility helps drive categories down the socio-economic pyramid; the corporatisation of the film industry made stars available; and pre-testing rewards celebrity presence.

whole_system_claim.text: Celebrity saturation is over-determined: several independent forces each push the same way, so no single one of them needs to be the cause, and at least one of them — the pre-test — pushes for reasons unconnected to whether the advertising works.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The author does list these as reasons, in sequence, in one passage ("The answer may lie somewhere else… The second reason is… One final reason…"), so the membership and the ordering are his. What is the extractor's is the over-determination claim: the observation that the forces are independent of one another and that this makes the phenomenon insensitive to any one of them. The author draws no such conclusion.
whole_system_claim.source_ref: Ch. 'Meri Khubsurti Ka Raaz', 'Why this celebrity obsession, you may ask.'

evidence.system_level_uncertainty:
Moderate. The membership and sequence are the source's own — he enumerates the reasons — so unlike the other three systems here the grouping is not invented. The over-determination reading is the extractor's.

item.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
item.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Awareness: Get noticed"; section "Core ABCDs", rows "Attention", "Branding" and "Connection"
item.question: A 20-second ad for a new energy drink opens on a silent slow-motion product beauty shot, brings the logo up only at the very end, shows no people at all, and closes on a "Buy now" end card. The brief is an awareness campaign. Judged strictly by this source, what is wrong with it — and what is not?
item.answer: Three of the four awareness instructions are missed. Attention for awareness is to be won with audio ("Pump up the volume by using audio to get viewers to pay attention") and the opening is silent. Branding is to be "front and center" and the brand arrives last, which also fails the core guideline to show up early and throughout. Connection is to "Make the people core to the story", and there are no people, which also fails the core guideline to humanise the story. What is not wrong on this source's terms is the end card: awareness is the one row where Direction is left at "Apply core principles", and the core guidance asks only that a CTA be present and intentionally chosen for a specific objective. The source gives no basis for calling the ask misplaced or over-strong here, and asserting one would go beyond it.
item.support: Awareness row: audio-led attention, brand front and centre, people core to the story, Direction at core. Core rows supply the early-and-throughout and humanise guidelines.
confounders: criticising the 'Buy now' CTA as wrong for awareness — a reasonable marketing instinct that this source does not support
citing 'Jump in' against the slow-motion opening; the source's pacing guidance is about reaching the story's point, and a beauty shot is not judged on speed alone
assuming a product-led ad satisfies Branding; the source's awareness instruction is about the brand being front and centre, and its Branding guidance asks for variety of asset

item.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
item.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Connection", guideline "Focus the message", and row "Attention", guideline "Support the story with audio and supers"; row "Attention", guideline "Jump in"
item.question: An ad packs three separate product benefits into fifteen seconds, each with its own voice-over line and its own super, over fast cutting. Which named faults does this source say it hits, under which principles — and which element of the description does the source not object to?
item.answer: Two named faults, under two different principles. "Doing too much" under Connection, from "Focus the message: Avoid doing too much in your ad. Keep messaging and language focused and simple." And "competing elements" under Attention, from "Support the story with audio and supers: Reinforce your message with audio and text. Avoid competing elements." — three voice-over lines and three supers carrying three different messages are not reinforcing one message. The fast cutting is the element the source does not object to: engaging pacing is what it asks for under "Jump in". Neither fault is quantified anywhere — no message count, and no test for when two elements compete rather than reinforce — so the diagnosis is directional and the threshold would be the implementer's.
item.support: Both faults are named at the locators given; "engaging pacing" is part of the Jump in guideline.
confounders: condemning the fast cutting, which the source's own Attention guidance encourages
filing both faults under one principle
supplying a 'one message per ad' rule as if the source stated it

item.question: The source's Attention principle asks for two distinct things. What are they, and what means does it name for achieving them?
item.answer: Hooking attention and sustaining it — "Hook and sustain attention with an immersive story" — so an arresting opening that then loses the viewer does not satisfy the principle. The means named for both is audio and visuals together: "Drop viewers in from the start and immerse them with audio and visuals that pique their interest." The audio half is the one part of Attention for which the source gives a mechanism: music, voice-over and sound effects are said to create a rich, sensory experience that helps people pay attention. item.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
item.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Attention", guideline "Jump in"; Google for Business resources, section "B – Branding", sub-heading "Show up early and throughout"
item.question: You are asked to build an automated check for the source's "Jump in" guideline. Why can it not be run on individual frames, and what does the source fail to give you?
item.answer: Because what "Jump in" describes is a property of a span, not of a still: how quickly the ad reaches the heart of its story, and whether the pacing and framing across the opening draw the viewer in. No single frame carries any of that, so the unit of observation has to be the opening sequence at least. What the source fails to give you is every number the check would need — no target time to the heart of the story, no definition of what the heart of the story is, and no reference point for "faster", which is comparative with nothing to compare to. The only figure anywhere nearby is a five-second mention in an illustrative caption about when one ad introduced its brand, which is a different guideline and is not stated as a rule. A check built from this can be directional; any threshold in it is the implementer's.
item.support: "Jump in" names pacing and framing over the opening and gives no duration; the five-second figure belongs to the Weekendesk caption under "Show up early and throughout".
confounders: borrowing the five-second figure as a Jump in threshold; it belongs to a different guideline and to one example
treating tight framing as a per-frame property that makes the check frame-level — the guideline is about the opening's effect, not a single composition
assuming the source's video specs page supplies a timing rule; it covers specs and safe zones

item.claim: The source's named technique "Jump in" asks the ad to reach the heart of its story sooner than it otherwise would, and names two specific means of doing so: pacing that keeps the viewer engaged, and tight framing.

scope.conditions: Named as a core Attention guideline, before any objective-specific tailoring

caveats.text: "Faster" is comparative with no stated reference point, and the source gives no target time to the heart of the story. The instruction is directional only.

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Pacing and Sequencing (spine 6)
item.question: In a book with no consistent page structure, where can the structure live instead, on Samara's account?
item.answer: In time, across the sequence. He says unconventional layout strategies tend to be more experiential than expository, and so lend themselves to other ways of thinking about sequence and pace: visual elements may relate to each other in time as though in frames of a film, with an image moving across a format or changing from page to page and affecting images or text that appear later. This kinetic structure comes to be recognised and understood as the viewer experiences the succession of frames. He adds that decisions about ebb and flow will often still be driven by the content's requirement for sequential clarity, but that a designer may treat sequence and pace as an idea in itself that establishes how the content ought to be delivered.
item.support: "Pacing and Sequencing": unconventional strategies as more experiential than expository; elements relating in time as film frames; kinetic structure recognised through the succession of frames; sequence and pace as an organising idea.
confounders: assuming a layout without page structure has no structure at all
treating pacing purely as rhythm or variety rather than as a carrier of order
assuming content requirements are set aside — he says they often still drive the ebb and flow
